title: Maha Sarakham 2 Days 1 Night: Phra That Na Dun & Khmer Ruins
metaDesc: A relaxed 2-day, 1-night Maha Sarakham plan in Isan, Thailand: old-town temples and Kaeng Loeng Chan lake, then south to Phra That Na Dun and Khmer ruins Ku Santarat and Ku Ban Khwao, with real timings and food stops.
keywords: Maha Sarakham 2 days 1 night, Maha Sarakham itinerary, Phra That Na Dun, Ku Santarat, Ku Ban Khwao
intro: Maha Sarakham is a small, easy-to-walk town, and two days with one overnight is enough to catch both the good stuff in town and the old sites down in Na Dun district. Day one is the town itself: Wat Maha Chai, Kaeng Loeng Chan, and a lakeside cafe. Day two heads out of town to Phra That Na Dun and two Khmer ruins. This plan already lays out realistic timings, so you're not rushing or driving in pointless loops.

blocks.html: Maha Sarakham isn't the first place that comes to mind when you plan an Isan trip, but if you like old sites, temples, and the quiet feel of a university town, it fits a short 2-day, 1-night trip perfectly. The town is small and you can drive across it in a few minutes; the real standout sights sit down in Na Dun district to the south, around 60-65 km from town, which is why they anchor day two.

This plan works best if you drive yourself or rent a car in town, because the Khmer ruins and Phra That Na Dun are off the regular bus routes. Getting there and back on public transport is possible but eats a lot of time. If you don't have a car, the easiest option is to charter a car or hire a motorbike taxi just for day two.

items: Day 1 — around town Wat Maha Chai, the scripture hall over the water, the old market, Kaeng Loeng Chan, a lakeside cafe, and a night market to finish.
Day 2 — south for history Ku Ban Khwao, then on to Na Dun for Phra That Na Dun and Ku Santarat before looping back to town.
Total driving under 20 km in town on day one; about 150 km round trip on day two. Allow around 3 hours on the rural roads.

blocks.html: Take day one easy and cover the in-town sights, which all sit close together; it's just a few minutes' drive from one to the next. Start at the town's landmark temple and end with sunset over the reservoir.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: In town — temples, markets, the reservoir

items.activity: Start the morning with khao piak sen (rice noodle soup) or congee near the municipal market
items.note: Breakfast spots in town open from before dawn until late morning. Isan-style breakfast is easy to find along Nakhon Sawan and Phadung Withi roads.

items.activity: Wat Maha Chai (Wat Nuea) — see the scripture hall over the pond and the local Isan museum
items.note: A landmark temple since 1865. The wooden scripture hall in the middle of the pond stored palm-leaf manuscripts over a hundred years old, and the temple museum keeps everyday Isan folk objects. Free to visit.

items.activity: Walk the old market and pick up local souvenirs like mam (Isan fermented sausage) and Isan sausage
items.note: Mam is one of the province's signature products, and several long-running shops have sold it for over 40 years. You can buy it vacuum-packed to take in the car.

items.activity: Lunch on punchy Isan food at Lao Niyom, Soi 4, Si Sawat Damnoen Road
items.note: Standouts are tam Lao (Lao-style papaya salad), fish soup, fresh-water crab salad, and crispy fried river shrimp, roughly 40-150 THB a plate. It's a place locals actually eat at.

items.activity: Escape the afternoon heat at a cafe with a coffee
items.note: November Cafe does homemade bread in town and is open 10:00-18:00 — a good spot to rest before heading out to Kaeng Loeng Chan.

items.activity: Kaeng Loeng Chan — the reservoir and public park in town, for a walk in the cool breeze
items.note: The city's green lung, with a walking and running path along the water and bikes to rent for the views. Several cafes ring the lake, like White Balance, a white-toned spot known for matcha, and Farmsook, a Japanese-style cafe with a kids' zone.

items.activity: Catch sunset over Kaeng Loeng Chan from a lakeside cafe
items.note: The evening light is lovely here, and it's a photo spot locals like to come and hang out at.

items.activity: Dinner at the Maha Sarakham municipal night market
items.note: The town's night market has a wide spread of food — savory dishes, sweets, and Isan fare — all at easy prices, and you can graze your way through it.

blocks.title: A tip on where to stay
blocks.html: Most accommodation clusters in town near the university and the market, so staying in town for the single night is the most convenient choice. Wake up on day two and drive straight south to Na Dun — no need to change hotels.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Khmer ruins and Phra That Na Dun

blocks.html: Day two is a full history day. Leave town heading south, stop first at Ku Ban Khwao near town, then push down to Na Dun, which has Phra That Na Dun and Ku Santarat in the same area. Ordering the route this way means you never have to double back.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Na Dun — Khmer sanctuaries and the Isan Buddhist park

items.activity: Leave town and stop at Ku Ban Khwao (Ku Maha That), 13 km out on Chaeng Sanit Road
items.note: A square, tower-shaped laterite Khmer sanctuary from around the 13th century, an old Khmer temple. Stop for photos and a quick respect-paying; it won't take long.

items.activity: Drive on to Na Dun district via Wapi Pathum, roughly 60-65 km from town
items.note: The route runs past rice fields and villages — easy driving, but they're rural roads, so allow extra time and fill up on fuel before you leave town.

items.activity: Phra That Na Dun — the Isan Buddhist park and Dvaravati-style stupa
items.note: Open 08:00-20:00. The stupa stands 50.5 meters tall on a 35.7-meter-wide base, designed by the Fine Arts Department after Dvaravati stupa forms. The grounds spread over 900 rai, with a botanical garden and herb garden — shady and pleasant to walk.

items.activity: Lunch at a local eatery around Na Dun
items.note: Na Dun has made-to-order spots and small Isan eateries around the district market — simple food at local prices.

items.activity: Ku Santarat — a laterite Khmer sanctuary from the reign of Jayavarman VII
items.note: Open 08:00-18:00. It was an arokayasala (a roadside Khmer hospital/rest house), with a square main prang facing east and an ancient reservoir outside called a baray. It's close to Phra That Na Dun, so it's an easy add-on.

items.activity: Nakhon Champa Si Historical Study Center — the story of the ancient city around Na Dun
items.note: It helps piece together why this area has both Dvaravati and Khmer remains, a good way to close out the history day before heading back.

items.activity: Drive back into Maha Sarakham town
items.note: Allow about 1.5 hours for the return, getting you to town just before evening.

items.activity: A final dinner in town and pick up any souvenirs you still need
items.note: If you haven't bought mam or local dried goods yet, stop at a souvenir shop in town before you leave.

blocks.text: What to know before you go

items: Opening hours differ Phra That Na Dun is open until 20:00, but Ku Santarat closes at 18:00, so do the ruins in the early afternoon to be safe.
Strong sun The Khmer ruins are open and exposed, so bring a hat and water. Midday sun is harsh; the best light for photos is early morning and late afternoon.
Fuel up in town Gas stations are spread out on the Na Dun side, so a full tank before leaving town gives you peace of mind.
Dress code Phra That Na Dun is a sacred site — dress modestly and don't wear spaghetti straps or short shorts into the stupa grounds.

blocks.title: If you have an extra half day
blocks.html: It stretches comfortably to 3 days, 2 nights. Add Maha Sarakham University and the student-dorm district, where food is cheap and plentiful, or stop at more of the province's Khmer ruins along its Khmer trail. See the longer plan in the sister article below.

faq.q: Is 2 days and 1 night enough for Maha Sarakham?
faq.a: It's enough to catch the highlights. Day one covers the town — Wat Maha Chai, Kaeng Loeng Chan, cafes, and the night market — and day two heads south to Phra That Na Dun and the Khmer ruins. If you also want to see the university and add more ruins, stretch it to 3 days, 2 nights.

faq.q: How far are Phra That Na Dun and Ku Santarat from town?
faq.a: They're in Na Dun district, south of the province, about 60-65 km from town, roughly a 1 to 1.5 hour drive. Both sit in the same area, so you can see them back to back in one day.

faq.q: Can I do this without my own car?
faq.a: In town you can walk and take a taxi, but there's no direct public transport on the Na Dun side. The advice is to charter a car or hire a motorbike taxi just for day two — it's far better value on time than waiting for several connecting rides.

faq.q: What's the difference between Ku Santarat and Ku Ban Khwao?
faq.a: Ku Santarat is in Na Dun district, a Bayon-style Khmer arokayasala from the reign of Jayavarman VII. Ku Ban Khwao (Ku Maha That) is near town on Chaeng Sanit Road, a tower-shaped laterite sanctuary. You can stop at Ku Ban Khwao on the way out of town, which fits the route nicely.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Maha Sarakham?
faq.a: Late rainy season into the cool season, roughly November to February, when the weather is pleasant and walking the open-air ruins isn't too hot. The hot season from March to May has harsh sun, so stick to mornings and evenings.
